1.explanation:
• src/ol/layer/Graticule.js implements the generation of meridians and parallels based on the view extent and projection. Its logic for computing longitude ranges (minLon → maxLon) does not handle cases where maxLon < minLon (i.e. crossing the 180° meridian), so grid lines are omitted or drawn across the wrong span.

• src/ol/proj/Projection.js stores each projection’s world extent, wrap settings, and computes normalized coordinates. When the view crosses the antimeridian, the world-extent orientation and wrapX flag must be consulted to split the grid, but the current code never triggers a split.

• src/ol/proj/transforms.js contains the low-level transform functions that normalize longitudes into [−180°, +180°] ranges. These normalization steps collapse the wrapped range, so positions beyond the dateline wrap back in a way that the graticule code cannot detect a crossing.

• src/ol/coordinate.js (toStringHDMS and related formatters) are used by Graticule.js to turn numeric lat/long into label strings. When longitudes get normalized incorrectly, the formatter sees values like ±170° in the wrong hemisphere or even out-of-range values, leading to garbled or duplicated label text.

Together, these files govern how the grid coordinates are computed, wrapped, and labeled. All must be updated so that when the map extent straddles the antimeridian, the longitude range is split into two segments (one on each side), grid lines are generated for both, and labels are formatted from the un-wrapped longitude values.
1.bug_scenario: When the map’s view projection crosses the antimeridian (±180°), most meridians never get drawn and the parallels start or end abruptly at the dateline or extend too far. Labels in some reprojection cases even become garbled. In the first screenshot, only a handful of the expected meridians appear west of Alaska, and the parallels jump at the 180° line. In the second, label text is mis-encoded and repeats improperly. The root cause is that the graticule generator assumes a continuous longitude range and a single global extent; it fails to split or wrap the grid when the view extent straddles the dateline.

2.explanation:
1. src/ol/layer/Graticule.js
   • This is the core implementation of the graticule layer: it computes meridian and parallel coordinates based on the view extent, transforms them into the view projection, and builds the line geometries and labels. The bug—missing meridians when the extent crosses the date line—originates here because the code assumes minLon < maxLon without handling a split at ±180°. Fixing it requires changing Graticule.js to detect when the view extent wraps around the dateline and to generate two sets of lines (one on each side) or to normalize longitudes correctly before line interpolation.

2. src/ol/proj/common.js
   • This module provides helper functions for wrapping and normalizing longitudes (e.g. wrapX functionality) and for computing world extents. The graticule code relies on these common utilities when it transforms geographic coordinates for display. Adjusting or adding functions here will allow Graticule.js to query and handle wrapped extents properly (for example, splitting an extent that crosses the date line into two contiguous ranges).

3. src/ol/proj/transforms.js
   • All coordinate transformations between projections are registered here, including normalization of input and output longitudes. Because the graticule generation feeds raw lat/long values through these transforms, any automatic normalization (e.g. forcing longitudes into [−180°, 180°]) can inadvertently collapse lines that should straddle the date line. Patching this file (or its registration of wrapExtent behavior) will ensure meridians and parallels maintain continuity across the boundary when Graticule invokes transform operations.
2.bug_scenario: When the map view projection crosses the 180° meridian (the international date line), the Graticule layer fails to draw most of the meridian lines and the latitude parallels start or end at the date line instead of extending across the entire view. In the provided screenshot (US National Atlas projection crossing the date line), you can see large gaps in the longitude lines between 120° W and 160° E, and the latitude lines abruptly stop at the date line. This is because the code that computes and renders graticule lines assumes a single continuous numeric range for longitude, but when the view extent spans the −180°/180° boundary it needs to split or wrap the grid lines properly.
